newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's headcount runs into problems.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's headcount runs into problems.

text.p: South Africa's first post- apartheid census has been marred by harassment and intimidation in some areas with one enumerator abducted and raped, government officials said on Tuesday.

Marinda de Lange, spokeswoman for the Central Statistical Service (CSS) which began conducting the three-week operation five days ago, said some of the 80,000 enumerators had been confronted by groups demanding to do the counting themselves.

"The census is proceeding very well, although our enumerators have been prevented from counting people in some areas by groups claiming to be unemployed and wanting to be employed as enumerators," she said in an interview.

The 356 million rand ($78.5 million) exercise will for the first time try to accurately tally the country's blacks, whose numbers were estimated in previous apartheid-era counts from aerial photographs of their settlements.
One enumerator was abducted and raped by unknown assailants in a black settlement in the province of Mpumalanga and some batches of census forms have been set on fire there.
Kobus van Wyk, spokesman for the census in Mpumalanga, said police had been asked to escort census workers in dangerous areas.
"The big problem here many people think the census is a job creation scheme. Some of them have even paid money to unions which promised to get them the job," he said.
"Most people want to be counted and we cannot tolerate troublemakers who have even unleashed dogs on some of our workers," van Wyk added.
CSS head Mark Orkin described the problems as minor. "We are confident...of the process and ultimate success of the first population count in a democratic South Africa," he said in a statement.
He said problems had also arisen from racial classification options on the census forms which ask people to describe themselves as black, white, Coloured or Asian.
The Griqua community in the Northern Cape, who regard themselves as a unique ethnic group, objected to this and have threatened to boycott the census.
"When the census data is processed these communities will be listed as sub-groups," Orkin said.
Early figures from the census are expected by the end of November. It is hoped they will provide vital information on unemployment, education and housing needs.
